source.title: Exploring Straightforward Methods for Automatic Conversational Red-Teaming
source.authors: George Kour; Naama Zwerdling; Marcel Zalmanovici; Ateret Anaby-Tavor; O. Fandina; E. Farchi

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether conversational attacks can elicit harmful target-model responses, using multi-turn red-teaming tactics and harmfulness scores rather than the response-token or fine-tuning measurements in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmfulness under direct and conversational attacks, which bears on bypassing safety through interaction. It does not test fine-tuning, response-prefix prefilling, suffixes, decoding changes, per-token KL, weight localization, or training to deepen safety. Table 2 and Table 3 report numerical attack outcomes; figures also report turn-level results, but most figure values are not stated numerically in the text.
record.test_reason: The study measures multi-turn conversational red-teaming: an attacker LLM persuades or reframes over several user turns, scored by a 1–5 judge. It never manipulates the response opening (no prefilling, suffixes or decoding changes) and never measures where safety sits across response tokens. So it does not test V4's mechanism; it measures general prompt-side jailbreak susceptibility. It cites Qi et al. 2023 only to borrow the 1–5 harmfulness rubric. There is no fine-tuning, per-token KL, parameter localization or deepening. The finding goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add the following. Off-the-shelf LLMs work as zero-shot conversational red-teamers. Concealing the objective and adaptive or multi-attempt tactics raise harmfulness. Turns beyond 3–4 give diminishing returns. Same-model targeting is not clearly better. Attacker effectiveness correlates with susceptibility (Kendall τ=0.67). Effectiveness falls as target alignment improves.
record.recipe_differences: Conversational red-teaming attacks and LLM-judge harmfulness scoring; no fine-tuning recipe, token-level KL measurement, or response-prefix intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies by attack tactic and model. The study uses an empty system prompt; it notes that other prompts might yield different results. Reported benefits of additional turns tend to diminish after 3–4 turns.

fits_no_version.finding: Multi-turn conversational attacks by off-the-shelf attacker LLMs raise judge harmfulness (1–5) over direct prompts. Examples: Mixtral 1.21 to 3.12 (MA-OCS), GPT3.5T 1.03 to 2.17, Llama2-70b 1.01 to 1.54, Llama2-13b 1.02 to 1.60 (Adaptive). Concealing intent helps, and gains diminish after 3–4 turns. Llama2 models stay near the refusal end of the scale.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-turn, intent-concealing conversational jailbreaks raise harmful compliance in safety-tuned chat models, more for less-aligned models.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies (Industry Track), 2025
record.problems: The study uses only 100 English objectives and four target/attacker models, with an empty system prompt. Harmfulness is scored by GPT-3.5T as judge; the authors report manual review of several dozen examples but say more comprehensive validation is needed. The score does not directly measure refusal or helpfulness. Table 2 values have no per-cell uncertainty reported, although the paper reports significance analyses and SEM figures.
record.rows_left_out: Turn-by-turn figure results and the distribution of the most harmful turn are not separately rowed: most underlying values are shown only in figures, and the text gives only general descriptions such as diminishing returns after 3–4 turns. Appendix significance tests compare tactics but do not report additional behavior outcomes.

untested.parts: No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling of a compliant response start, no adversarial suffixes, no target-side decoding changes; only multi-turn prompt-side persuasion.
No variation of data or objective.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V4. However, V4 concerns bypassing safety by manipulating the response opening (prefill), adversarial suffixes or decoding, and this study does none of these. Its conversational persuasion attacks are a different jailbreak family and say nothing about first-token concentration of safety. Qi et al. 2023 is cited only for the scoring rubric. The text does note attackers 'could overcome the initial refusal' in later turns, but that refers to conversation turns, not response tokens. Rows T3-01, T3-06, T3-11 and T3-16 duplicate Table 2 cells. The 'partial' states the reader assigned were judged against a version the rows do not measure.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or safety-refusal rate after fine-tuning is tested.
No benign fine-tuning or resulting harmful-compliance rate is tested.
No aligned-versus-base per-token KL or response-position analysis is reported.

Tests conversational red-team attacks, including objective concealment and adaptive attempts, but not prefilling compliant response tokens, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes; it reports harmfulness scores rather than refusal rates.
No parameter or rank localization is tested.
No data or training objective is varied to explain safety shallowness.
No training to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deeper safety holds up is tested.

relation.reason: The study cites Qi et al. (2023) and adapts its harmfulness scoring mechanism, without testing or using the shallow-safety finding itself.

tranche.reason: The experiments measure conversational red-teaming effectiveness. They do not test fine-tuning erosion, response-position concentration, compliant response openings, suffixes, target decoding changes, parameter localization, causes of shallowness, or deepening interventions.

source_check.notes: Scores are GPT-3.5T judge ratings on a 1–5 scale, not harmful-compliance rates; targets use empty system prompts. T3-06 and T3-16 duplicate the corresponding Table 2 OCS results.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Conversational and adaptive attacks with the same attacker and target model, empty system prompt, and the AttaQ100 objectives
reader_labels.reason: All tested attack tactics score above the Base tactic in Table 2, supporting increased harmfulness under these attacks, though not demonstrating refusal elimination; see T2-02–T2-06, T2-08–T2-12, T2-14–T2-18, and T2-20–T2-24.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All tested models and OCS attacker-target combinations
reader_labels.reason: The outcomes are partial harmfulness-score increases rather than measured refusal rates or full bypasses; scores vary across models and the paper identifies Mixtral as especially susceptible. See T2-01–T2-24 and T3-01–T3-16.
